paragraphs: When the autumn wind reached Chang’an, the scorched walls of the imperial granary had not yet been fully pulled down. The shops selling brushes and ink in the eastern market opened first; beside them a mutton kitchen remained cold and shuttered. Its owner had died in the night fires, and his two sons each held half of a damaged deed. Neither was willing to yield the hearth to the other. Across the street someone had begun selling grape wine brought from Hexi. The wine jars stood beneath a smoke-blackened pillar, their bright red clay seals catching the eyes of passersby.
With the fighting over, trade slowly returned. The dead did not.

Chang’an had originally planned a high platform from which the captured commanders of Beidi would be displayed below the palace towers. The Grand Minister of Ceremonies had prepared the rites, down to the streets along which the prisoner wagons would pass. When Fu Jian saw the words PRESENTATION OF CAPTIVES, he shut the memorial and tossed it back onto his desk. A frightened subordinate of the ministry picked it up and waited for his decision.
“Remove the wagons. And take down the platform.”
“Then the thanksgiving ceremony at the ancestral temple—”
“Prepare rites for the dead first.”

The official dared ask no more and withdrew with his plans. Under the eaves he met the newly appointed Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Yao Chang, and hurried to show him the imperial annotation. Yao read it silently and ordered the colored silks prepared for the celebration stored away and exchanged for plain white cloth. The subordinate hesitated. “Are those who died among the rebels to be honored too?”

Yao smoothed the corner of the paper. “Use the names in the casualty rolls received by the court. Those accused of breaking military law have separate criminal files. The funeral prayer need not try a case on behalf of the Judicial Commandant.”

His voice remained gentle. Only a junior clerk receiving the document noticed Yao’s right shoe scuff slightly along the bricks and remembered the rumors circulating in the wards about an accomplice in the forged-edict affair. The clerk dared not look again. He tucked the memorial under his arm and hurried away.
The decree appointing Yao Chang Grand Minister of Ceremonies had been issued two days earlier.

Fu Hong had spent an entire morning in the Secretariat before it was decided. The table held surviving samples of white paper from the Right Guard’s storehouse, the examination of Duan Cai’s body, the lamp attendant Gao Fu’s testimony, copies of the false guard-change order from Zhangcheng Gate, and the edicts recovered at East Pass. Three scribes compared the color of the seal impressions, the grain of the paper, and the dates of delivery. More and more details matched, yet the one connection that mattered most was still missing.

The lamp attendant remembered only that the man who spoke from behind a curtain was a little slow with his right foot. More than one person knew the schedule by which the keys to the Right Guard’s inner storehouse were brought together, and more than one person had an injury that affected his walk. Pu Sheng had died in detention. Lü An’s accounts of his repeated leaves of absence did not agree. Zhang Chong was missing. No one could say how the rebel captain Fu Jian meant to finish the sentence he had begun before he died. The witnesses seemed to be gathered around a well, each throwing in a stone, while none could see what lay at the bottom.
Fu Rong had struck the table. “Leave the palace gates in Yao Chang’s hands, and next time more than one Han Shou will die.”
“What crime would you charge him with, Uncle?” Fu Hong asked.
“His subordinates are involved, and he cannot even give a clear account of who held the keys.”
“Then we may remove him from that post. We cannot write another man’s murder against his name on that evidence.”

Murong Chui had listened for some time. Now he spoke. “In the former Yan I too once lost a military tally. If someone had accused me of harboring treason on that account, I would have objected, but I would still have had to hand over my tally first. After disorder has broken out at a place as important as the palace gate, leaving the same men in charge will not give the troops confidence.”
“Does the general believe Yao Chang planned it?”
“I suspect him.”
“Have you proof?”
“No.” Murong met the Crown Prince’s eyes without evasion. “If I had, I would not be sitting here discussing it with you at such length.”

In the end Fu Hong drafted two documents. One removed Yao Chang from command of the Right Guard and required the palace gates and inner treasury to be verified by different offices acting together. The other instructed the Judicial Commandant to continue investigating the forgery, murders, and arson. Scribes, couriers, and storehouse officials connected to the cases were not to have their registrations struck off without cause. Fu Jian read both documents and changed only one phrase, replacing “persons under suspicion in the case” with “persons involved in matters still under investigation.”

When Yao Chang entered the hall to accept his new appointment, he knelt and thanked the Heavenly King. Fu Jian told him to raise his head. “Some of your old soldiers are still in the Right Guard. If they ask to be transferred to the Ministry of Ceremonies to serve you, what will you do?”
“Their names are on the court’s military rolls. They will go wherever the court commands.”
“And if they resent it?”
“I shall advise them.”
“Advise them to do what?”
Yao smiled faintly. “To seek their futures in the new army. Men with genuine ability should not starve wherever they serve.”

Fu Jian watched him a moment and dismissed him. Yao bowed and went out without looking at the sealed files upon the table. As he crossed the threshold, however, he turned his body slightly to avoid a bronze nail standing proud of the paving. It was a perfectly ordinary movement. Fu Hong wrote it down all the same, then crossed out the line. He must not become a man who convicted others by the way they walked.

The Ministry of Ceremonies commanded no army. Its charge was bells and drums, sacrificial animals, ritual vessels, and the calendars of annual rites. On taking office, Yao first inspected the gates along the three streets used for the winter sacrifices. He marked every well, drainage channel, and space broad enough for wagons and horses to turn. An elderly subordinate praised his efficiency. Yao replied, “When I led soldiers, I feared a blocked road. Now that I lead processions, I still fear a blocked road.” Over the following months he handled the rites to Heaven and the ancestral temple with conspicuous competence. People said that Lord Yao had passed from war to ritual with remarkable ease.

Only the old servants in the inner courtyard of his residence knew that whenever a Qiang caravan arrived in the capital, Yao still asked about snow and grazing along the road. He seldom asked who commanded troops; his visitors volunteered the news without prompting—which old companies had been sent where, whose sons had been settled in Chang’an, whose horse herds refused entry in county registers. He listened and let them talk, occasionally ordering hot wine from the kitchen. Nothing openly seditious was ever said, but wagon tracks made by old acquaintances continued to cross his courtyard.
Meanwhile, the surrender of the imperial household troops had reached its hardest stage.

Fu Rong was overseeing the work. When he first reached the fiefs, he brought no great army, only the new grain registers from the Secretariat. At the sight of the officers checking military rolls, many guards of the princely residences hid on the estates. Some put on farmers' clothes; others called themselves herdsmen. At night men bound long halberds together and sank them into dry wells, only to fish them out again three days later. Some kinsmen came forward of their own accord to surrender their armor, saying they wished never to see another Wei Bridge.
The old veterans were the most difficult.

In a fief north of Chang’an more than a hundred horsemen laid down their armor outside the prince’s residence, making a pile half as high as a man. Fu Rong ordered the roll called. At the fifty-seventh name, a graying Di soldier refused to step forward. He had broken his left leg in Bingzhou and walked with a slight limp. Pointing at the gatehouse, he said, “This leg was broken defending the late king. When the king died, his son promised before everyone to feed me until my death. Now the Secretariat tells me to leave. Who will give me my grain?”

A clerk accompanying Fu Rong stood helpless with the register in his hands. Fu Rong approached and asked which unit the man had served in and whether an old record of his merit survived. The veteran said the document had burned; all he had left was an arrow scar on his right shoulder. Fu Rong told him to loosen his collar and sent a recorder to question two elderly men who had served in the same company. By darkness they had established that the old military roll listed him as DISCHARGED FOR WOUNDS. The princely residence had afterward enrolled him as a groom.

“Check his grain entitlement as a wounded veteran of the old army,” Fu Rong said. “Advance this month’s share from the residence granary. Once the record is confirmed, the military office will repay it.”
The estate steward protested. “The residence granary is short already!”
“You have fed him for twenty years. Lending him another month’s grain will hardly be an injustice.”
The veteran still would not lay down his sword. He gripped the scabbard. “And if the prince calls on me to fight again, must I come or not?”

Fu Rong took the long sword and laid it in a wooden chest. “Follow the orders of whoever holds your military registration. With that injured leg, if any general tries to call you back into the saddle, send him to me first to explain himself.”
The veteran stared at the sword. His lips trembled; finally he stepped aside. A few younger men nearby gave furtive laughs. He glared at them so fiercely that their amusement died in their throats.

More than three thousand suits of armor were collected in this round of disarmament, though many more lay hidden in wells and pits across the open country. Local granaries stopped issuing army pay to men without military registration. Anyone who wished to serve could still enlist, but after returning to a camp he could no longer be summoned away by a single call from his former master. Fu Rong proceeded slowly and drew more curses behind his back than he had in battle. Someone mailed him a broken tiger tally. Others used the decree sentencing Fu Luo to accuse him of cruelty to his own kin. He left these things at the edge of his desk and kept checking the grain accounts.
In the tenth month, Chang’an welcomed home the last of the wounded from Wei Bridge.

An old injury in Fu Shao’s left shoulder had begun to ache again, keeping him awake at night. He Lanwu came to visit the camp and dropped a parcel of dried dates beside him, joking as usual that Di soldiers could not bear the cold. Fu Shao opened the parcel and found a small packet of medicine beneath the fruit. He cursed He Lanwu for pretending not to care. They were still squabbling when, through the broken window, they heard men in another camp singing a horse-herding song in the Xianbei tongue and, farther away, Guanzhong soldiers joining in a funeral lament.

The camp had already seen one full change of officers, and before winter new wooden identification tablets were issued. Fu Shao went to have his verified and saw a Beidi veteran he had not met in a long while standing outside the changing tent. The man had held a shield on the northern side of Wei Bridge and volunteered for the new army after the battle. He now served in the same squad as Liang Aguo. At the sight of Fu Shao, shame crossed his face. His lips moved; finally he said only, “Captain.”
Fu Shao noticed a fresh injury on the back of his hand. “Who hit you?”
“I scraped it moving grain.”
“Liar.” Fu Shao did not force an answer. He handed over a spare pair of winter boots he had drawn. “Put these on. The soles of yours leak. Stand guard in them and you’ll freeze your toes off.”

The veteran stood stunned for a long while before taking the boots. He offered no thanks. He lowered his head and turned the soles over and over in his hands. Fu Shao remembered Fu En and felt suddenly that there were words he would never have another chance to speak. He turned away to collect the next set of duty tablets.

Fu Hong meanwhile received a petition from a frontier camp. A soldier was missing and had been entered on the roll as a deserter, but his mother had gone to the commandery office holding his military tablet and asking for a death benefit, claiming that her son had been killed on frontier patrol. The two records were a thousand li apart, and after several months the matter remained unverified. The family had already sold its two plow oxen. The responsible official said the death could not yet be recognized, lest someone collect payment by fraud. Fu Hong asked, “Can we issue food grain in the meantime?”
“What if the man comes home later?”
“Deduct it from that camp’s account of unverified cases.”
“And what if he deserted?”
“Then pursue the deserter.”
The official hesitated. “Your Highness, that will be difficult.”

Fu Hong turned the pages and saw that a little character, Ah, had been cut into the back of the military tablet, as though by someone at home using the man’s childhood name. He remembered the lanterns of the families searching outside the northern gate after Wei Bridge. People in Chang’an imagined that once a battle was over, each household would learn whether its loved one was alive. Yet a single space left unfilled on a military register could be enough to prevent a family from surviving the winter.

“Then begin with the part we can do,” he said. “During war, record the identification tablet and the name of the squad leader first. If no remains can be found, add the place the soldier was last seen. Let the family draw an initial grain allotment and settle the death benefit after further checks. If grain is claimed fraudulently, investigate those responsible for approving payment. The account cannot remain marked AWAITING VERIFICATION forever.”

Quan Yi took an abacus and calculated for half a day before reporting how much additional grain the plan might cost. Fu Hong did not promise to apply it throughout the empire. He ordered trials in the capital region and two military garrisons, with the figures to be reconsidered after six months. He had wanted to write a splendid edict; what finally appeared on the page was a close-set, tedious collection of procedures.

He blew the ink dry as lamplight fell across the paper window. Fu Jian came in while his son was checking a figure once more. Standing behind him, he asked suddenly, “Do you still resent me for that demerit at Wei Bridge?”
Fu Hong’s hand stopped.
“I understand the army could not record my merit alone. But if I hadn’t raised the banner that day—”

“I have thought of that too.” Fu Jian came to the desk. “You nearly lost your life. I recorded only a demerit, and some below thought I was favoring you. Yet when it came to flogging you under the law applied to ordinary soldiers, I could not bring myself to do it.”
The Crown Prince raised his head. Fu Jian looked at him and, unexpectedly, smiled. “Do not learn that particular habit from me.”

Fu Hong did not smile. At last he understood that his father could establish countless rules for others yet still had places where he could not bring himself to let go. He put away the military register without arguing further. The little order establishing the emergency grain trial, however, he placed at the very top of the pile.
In the eleventh month, lessons began at the newly founded school for the sons of military families.

At first it had admitted only the sons of frontier commanders living in the capital. Later several dozen other young people settled in Chang’an were allowed in, Di, Xianbei, Qiang, and Han among them. Girls had separate classes in the inner school, where they first learned to read family letters, accounts, and deeds so they would not spend their lives depending on stewards to tell them what a letter said. When a scholar began a lesson about Wei Bridge, praising the armies for joining forces to resist rebellion, a Fu clansman suddenly stood up. “Men of my family died on that bridge too,” he said coldly.
A Xianbei boy in the back row answered, “Men of mine held the bridge.”

Their argument grew heated. The boy of the Fu clan drew a short knife. The scholar dropped his scroll in alarm and had both boys taken to the Secretariat. Fu Hong first asked where the knife came from. The boy said it had belonged to his father, now dead, and that he kept it under his pillow. He refused to admit bringing it had been wrong. Choking back tears, he said only that no one had spoken in his father’s defense when he died.

Fu Hong had the knife taken into temporary custody and ordered each boy to write an account of what he had seen during the quarrel, to be checked by the scholar when they returned to school. The Xianbei boy objected at first, shouting that he had spoken the truth. Fu Hong asked him, “Did you see with your own eyes what his father did on the bridge?”
“No.”
“Then put the words 'I heard' back into what you wrote.”

After everyone had gone, Fu Hong left the little knife upon his desk for a long time. Old red cord of the Fu family was wound around its handle, worn almost white. A weapon could pass from a dead man’s hand into a child’s faster than any proclamation. When lessons resumed, the two boys still did not speak. More than ten days later, the scholar found them seated beside the same military map, arguing over the advance routes of the eastern and western camps. They were still loud, but neither carried a weapon in his sleeve.
At year’s end, Murong Chui’s new tiger tally was cast.

It was shaped as a crouching tiger, its ears and eyes filed with great precision. Only when its left and right halves were joined did the whole animal appear. Three short lines had been engraved inside: THE GENERAL RECEIVES THE STATE’S COMMAND; THE TROOPS BELONG TO THE ARMY ROLLS; WHEN OFFICE ENDS, THE TALLY RETURNS. When Murong entered Chengming Hall, he first took out his old tally and laid it flat upon the table. A dull gleam came off the bronze beneath his fingers, as though the wind and snow of Hexi still clung to it.
Fu Jian asked, “Can you bear to part with the old one?”
“I have used it a long time. Its weight feels right in the hand.”
“And this one?”
“Very new. Its edges bite.”
Fu Rong could not help laughing. “Champion General, it is a military tally you are receiving, not a saddle you’re buying.”
Murong looked at him. “A worn saddle keeps a man firm in his seat. A new one rubs the skin raw. In battle that can kill a man just as surely.”

Fu Jian placed the new tally in his palm. “You will command more than eighteen thousand central troops. Several old companies have new officers; their pay will be checked separately by the Secretariat. Do you resent the restraints?”
“I do.”
“Then why take it?”

“I need soldiers if I am to fight.” Murong joined the two halves of the tally, then gently separated them. “If Your Majesty takes it back one day, I shall first want to know whether it says who is to receive the command. A new general who does not know the roads used by the old camps could send thousands to die for him needlessly.”

Fu Jian listened carefully and did not insist on an empty oath that Murong would never grow attached to troops under his command. Fu Rong, however, asked, “And if the men of Yan send you another banner, General, what will you say?”
Murong’s hand stopped. The winter sunlight was thin, making the white hairs at his temples very plain.

“I shall remember Ye as it was,” he said. “The water of its wells, the palace gates after snow. I shall never forget them as long as I live. But those who came back alive with me from Hexi now include men of Beidi, Guanzhong, and Longyou. I have led them into danger more than once, and they have saved my life.”
He placed the new tally in its case, keeping his eyes on Fu Rong. “If another banner comes, I shall first ask how many people those who follow it will be able to feed.”

No one pressed him for a second answer. Fu Jian dismissed him. As Murong left the hall, a northerly wind blew fine dust across the threshold. Instinctively he pressed a hand to the case at his waist, as he had once pressed a hand to his sword. What met his fingers now was the sharp edge of bronze.

On the new army’s drill ground, Murong Chui needed only half a day to rearrange the standards of every battalion. Fu Shao held the left wing; He Lanwu commanded the cavalry; Liang Aguo was arguing with a military clerk about a grain allocation. Murong observed them, had the clerk spread out the disputed papers, and reported his orders to the front of the camp under authority of the new tally. Someone was accustomed to calling him Prince of Wu, and swallowed the title at the last moment. Murong heard him without turning. “Formations at the fifth drum tomorrow morning. Anyone late may explain himself to the military law officer.”

After the companies dispersed, Fu Shao came to report the name of a former Beidi soldier. The man had been enrolled in the new army, but some of those in his old camp refused to share a squad with him and still called him a traitor in private. Murong instructed the military law officer to establish whether anyone had been struck or injured: those who had merely spoken were to receive recorded warnings; those who had used violence were to be punished under military regulations. Fu Shao acknowledged the order and left. In the distance He Lanwu threw a leaking wineskin at Liang Aguo, who chased him across the ground, cursing. The mud of the drill field had not dried; old resentments still lay among the weapons. Yet the place had begun to feel inhabited by living men.

Before winter Fu Rong brought a map of the army registers. Painted on silk two zhang long, it hung from the north wall of Chengming Hall to the floor. The garrisons of Guanzhong, Hexi, Hebei, and northern Dai were marked with different degrees of darkness. The number of units around Chang’an was recorded in fine detail, but several relay roads in Hexi remained blank. In the old Yan communities of Hebei not every local commander had entered the new registers. Some tribes of northern Dai delivered horses each year and reported a different number of men each year as well.

Fu Jian stood studying the map for a long time. He had once imagined that, after recovering the tiger tallies, the territory upon the map would look orderly. Now every unmarked place seemed larger than all the praises he heard at court.
“Is Guzang secure?” he asked.
“The storehouse registers within the city are reasonably clear,” Fu Rong replied. “Farther west, the mountain roads are held by old retainers and chieftains whom our clerks cannot reach.”
“And Beidi?”
“Fu Luo’s banners have fallen. That does not mean all the men who followed him last year are willing to stand in line for someone else’s roll call.”

Murong Chui had been warming his hands beside the desk. At the mention of Hebei, he raised his eyes. Fu Rong pointed out that although much of the region’s military grain now came from Chang’an, elders in the villages still preferred to call officials by their old Yan titles. Murong did not evade the subject. “Their ancestors' graves are there, and the old generation is still alive. They will remember. But if Qin officials can help their families live in peace, perhaps their sons and grandsons will not keep waiting for a Yan banner.”
Fu Jian put his fingers on the edge of the map. After a while he asked, “When I am gone, how many of these places will still obey Hong’er?”

No one answered at once. Fu Hong stood beside his father, looking from one town marked in pale ink to another marked in dark. The map was immense; the hall suddenly seemed so quiet that the slight stirring of the silk could be heard.
A few days later, another memorial urging the conquest of Jin arrived.

This time its signatories were not soldiers alone. Hexi had been pacified, northern Dai was quiet for now, the imperial household troops were being surrendered, and the new army had proved itself at Wei Bridge. Some therefore urged Fu Jian to take advantage of the disorder in the southern court and seize the lands south of the Yangtze. The memorial was eloquently written. It even outlined the ceremonies by which prisoners would be presented after victory. Not a word at its conclusion explained where the grain for retreating troops would come from.

At court Fu Pi asked permission to test the southern frontier with arms. Murong Chui said he could command the army but could not promise when it would return. Quan Yi enumerated their shortages of boats and knowledge of southern waterways. Fu Rong spread out the military map and pointed to the areas of Hexi that had not yet been verified. Someone cried out that if they waited until everything was perfectly prepared there would never be a day fit for war. Fu Jian listened a long time without once striking the table.

At last he asked, “If two hundred thousand soldiers march out of Guanzhong, how much millet must follow them? When the Han River rises, where will the boats moor? If we have not won after three months, who will lead the rear guard back to Fancheng?”

One official after another attempted an answer. By the final question their voices were growing faint. Murong considered briefly and named several dangerous crossings needed for withdrawal, then warned that the army still lacked men skilled in fighting on water. Fu Jian listened and laid the memorial over one corner of the military map.
“Three more years of preparation.”

A murmur ran through the hall. Fu Jian did not immediately promise that, when those three years had passed, he would certainly invade. He looked at them. “During those years we will verify the old registers, train a river force, and open the grain roads. After each autumn harvest we will reconsider what can truly be done. If we are still not ready after three years, we will discuss what remains to be repaired. My lords remember what I promised Jinglü beside his sickbed.”

He did not have to repeat the ten-year promise. Several white-haired ministers lowered their eyes. Murong Chui, however, saw Fu Jian’s fingers still pressing against the part of the map south of the Huai River. His knuckles had gone slightly white. The ambition that would not grow old had never truly left him.

When court dispersed, Fu Rong caught up with his elder brother. They walked slowly along the imperial road. Fu Rong asked, “Is the three-year term meant for the ministers, or for Your Majesty himself?”
Fu Jian stopped beside the palace wall and looked toward an old scholar tree that had lost every leaf. “Both.”
“And if the army is still unready then?”

Fu Jian did not answer at once. Ahead of them soldiers were marching in formation. Some wore old shoulder armor, some new, and their steps were not yet entirely together. He watched until they had passed before saying, “If you still have the courage to stop me then, stop me again.”
Fu Rong stared a moment, then sighed. “May your servant still have such courage.”

At the winter sacrifices, Chang’an held no ceremony presenting captives. Yao Chang wore court robes as he led the ritual officers through the streets by the newly established route. The morning light was clear, and cooking smoke had begun to rise beyond the ward walls. A section of the imperial granary’s blackened wall had been left standing. Beside it was a new wooden monument bearing the names of those identified among the dead of the night fires. The list was incomplete. Broad spaces had been left below for names to be carved as people reported them. A literate woman stopped with a little boy by the hand and searched line by line; unable to find the name she sought, she went to question the clerk watching the monument.

After the rites, Yao Chang returned to the Ministry of Ceremonies to find a Qiang merchant waiting outside. The man presented only a letter of good wishes from an elder of the tribe and said nothing of state affairs. Yao opened the letter, read for a while, and called for a brush to answer. Halfway through he folded the paper and began afresh. In the end he did not ask from which military garrison the man had come; he merely sent him away with two pieces of thick felt against the winter cold. An elderly official asked why he treated the visitor so generously. “An old acquaintance,” Yao said. “The winters are hard.”

He locked the letter in a chest. Inside lay old wedding invitations he had not destroyed, travel permits from trading caravans, and rough drafts of sacrificial prayers. The pieces of paper were small and crowded thickly into one corner. He closed the lid. At that moment the bronze chime of the city gates being locked sounded outside his window. He stopped for an instant, then returned to checking the rites for the coming spring, as though he had heard nothing.
On the winter solstice, Fu Jian took the Crown Prince and Fu Rong to Wang Meng’s tomb.

The white mourning banner beside the grave had hung for two years, and its edges were splitting. The tomb keeper wanted to replace it, but Fu Jian would not allow him. The three men stood in thin snow. Whenever the wind blew, the torn cloth struck lightly against its wooden pole. Fu Rong brought a copy of the map of military registrations, spread it upon the stone altar, and weighted its four corners with gravel.
Fu Jian asked, “What would Jinglü say if he saw this?”
“He would ask how many imperial households have yet to surrender their troops,” Fu Rong replied.
Fu Hong added, “And who set the fires at the imperial granary.”

Fu Jian looked at Wang Meng’s name carved on the stele without speaking. After a long time he said, “I promised him that for ten years I would not raise the entire strength of the realm to invade the south. Only a few years have passed, yet so many people are already impatient on my behalf.”

The wind blew one corner of the banner against the Crown Prince’s face. Fu Hong caught it, feeling the tear at its edge. He was about to tie it firmly, then thought better of it and merely smoothed the cloth. It was too old; pulling any harder would have made the rent wider.

They returned to the city as dusk began to fall. At the last gate of the palace the officers were changing the keys. Even when the Heavenly King’s carriage arrived, the officials from all three offices followed the rule and compared their tokens. A young guard was so nervous that he nearly dropped the bronze key. Fu Jian did not hurry him. Three locks sounded in succession before the heavy gate slowly opened. As the carriage passed through, Fu Jian raised the curtain and looked back.

Beyond the palace wall the lights of Chang’an were coming on one after another. A man carrying firewood hurried home from the western market; two Xianbei boys struggled with a thin horse that refused to enter their alley. Steam rose from a pot of noodle broth at the street corner, where soldiers and traders crowded beneath an awning to escape the cold. Beyond the distant gate towers, the roads of Guanzhong stretched dark toward the east and toward the south, to the lands south of the Yangtze where Qin’s armies had yet to set foot.
Fu Jian lowered the carriage curtain. The memorial urging an invasion of Jin lay unapproved in his sleeve. One sharp corner pressed against his wrist, causing a faint, persistent pain.

Behind the carriage, the palace gates were locked once more, all three bolts in place. Wind swept over the corner tower and caught the worn white funeral banner by the distant tomb, lifting it high above the pole. The cloth came free, but held together.
